transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. The E:09 code on your Bosch SMS25AW00G specifically indicates a flow-through heating element or heating circuit failure. In this model, there is no separate exposed heating element at the bottom; instead, the heater is built into the circulation pump assembly. Regarding cost: because the heater is integrated into the main wash pump, replacing it involves swapping out that entire assembly. It is not a cheap fix, but it is often worth doing if the rest of the machine is in good condition. Before we assume the part has failed, I need to confirm the symptom pattern. Please run an intensive or 65°C programme with a normal load. At the end of the cycle, are the dishes hot and steamy (meaning it heated), or still stone cold?
I've already run the hot programme and the eco one over the last few runs and both came out cold. Water mid-cycle was cold to touch too. I do have a multimeter if you want me to test the heater.

Thanks for confirming that. Since both the intensive and eco programmes resulted in stone-cold water mid-cycle and at the end, this suggests a genuine 'no-heat' fault rather than just poor drying. On your Bosch SMS25AW00G, there is no separate exposed heating element at the bottom of the tub. Instead, the heating element is built directly into the circulation pump assembly (the flow-through heater). The E:09 code strongly supports this, as it indicates a failure in that specific circuit. Before we conclude the part needs replacing, we should verify the electrical state of the heater itself to rule out a wiring issue or a sensor fault. Since you have a multimeter, please do the following: 1. Switch off the dishwasher at the mains and unplug it (or isolate the fuse).
2. Access the pump assembly at the bottom of the tub.
3. Set your multimeter to measure resistance (Ohms/Ω).
4. Place the probes on the two terminals that connect to the heating element within the pump assembly. If the reading is 'OL' or infinity, the heater inside the pump has failed and the entire circulation-pump/heater assembly will need replacing. If you get a reading in the 20–30 Ohm range, the heater itself is likely fine, and we should look at the temperature sensor or wiring next. Please let me know what your multimeter reads.

Ok, I've unplugged it and taken the panel off. Across the two heater terminals on the pump I get an open circuit, nothing at all. So does that mean the whole pump/heater unit needs replacing, and roughly what would that cost? It's 9 years old so I'm weighing up repair vs replace.

An open circuit (infinity/OL) on the terminals suggests that the heating element inside the pump assembly has failed. Because this is a flow-through design where the heater is built into the pump, you cannot replace just the heating coil; the entire circulation-pump/heater assembly must be replaced. Regarding cost and whether it’s worth fixing: 1. 2. 3. Given that your machine is 9 years old, this is a borderline decision. If the rest of the appliance (drain pump, spray arms, door seal) has been working well and it hasn't had major issues recently, checking the pump/heater assembly is generally considered worth doing to extend its life by another few years. However, if you have already dealt with other faults or are concerned about long-term reliability, a new machine might offer better energy efficiency and warranty cover. If you decide to proceed with the repair, ensure you isolate the appliance at the mains before disconnecting any electrical connectors from the pump.
The cost part of your reply came through blank, just '1. 2. 3.'. Roughly how much would the pump/heater assembly cost, and is it a job I could do myself?
